strengths: The central idea—performing early denoising steps at lower spatial resolutions and progressively increasing resolution—is intuitive, practically useful, and well matched to transformer-based diffusion models whose attention cost grows rapidly with token count.

The method achieves a substantial approximately 2× reduction in reported inference and training time relative to its full-resolution counterpart at the same number of sampling steps, while retaining broadly similar quality on several metrics.

The evaluation covers SD3.5 Medium and Large, 30K-prompt COCO and MJHQ evaluations, multiple automated metrics, human preference comparisons, and useful ablations of scale-wise training, timestep shifting, schedules, synthetic data, and PDM.
The paper is clearly organized, provides understandable diagrams and qualitative comparisons, and includes relevant implementation and runtime-measurement information.
Training a single model to handle multiple scales is appealing and avoids the multiple separately trained models commonly required by cascaded diffusion systems.
weaknesses: The main quality claims are overstated. SWD has substantially worse FID than several baselines—for example, 23.0 versus 14.3 for DMD2-SDXL on COCO and 13.6 versus 7.2 on MJHQ—while its advantages in PickScore and ImageReward are often small. The abstract's 2.5×–10× speedup claim also does not hold uniformly across the listed strong baselines.

The human evaluation uses only 128 prompts and does not report exact win/tie/loss counts, statistical tests, confidence intervals in numerical form, inter-rater agreement, or prompt-level variance. Consequently, statements about significant improvements are insufficiently supported.

The spectral motivation is demonstrated only through limited illustrative power spectra. There is no quantitative criterion connecting frequency masking to the selected resolution/timestep schedules, no systematic analysis across samples and timesteps, and no direct evidence that the hand-designed schedules are near optimal.

PDM's novelty and characterization are questionable. With the default linear kernel, Equation 2 merely matches the mean teacher feature over spatial tokens separately for each paired image; it discards spatial structure and higher-order information and is closer to a global feature-matching loss than general patch-distribution matching. Comparisons against established perceptual or feature-distillation losses are missing.

The efficiency comparison lacks important controls: an independently optimized full-resolution few-step baseline under the same latency/FLOP budget, stronger dynamic token or resolution-reduction methods, batch-size-one latency, memory usage, and FLOP accounting. The reported 'latency' is obtained by dividing batch-8 runtime and is therefore primarily a throughput measurement.

Reproducibility is incomplete: loss weights and precise loss definitions, optimizer settings, sampling of scale pairs and training timesteps, the two-step schedule, synthetic prompt/data construction, SD3.5-Large discriminator/PDM feature layers, seeds, and evaluation generation settings are not fully specified; no code or model-release commitment is given.

Generality remains limited despite broad claims. The main quantitative experiments use two sizes of the same SD3.5 family, while the claimed ability to handle SDXL at low resolutions is supported only qualitatively. Training also relies on 500K teacher-generated samples whose generation cost is excluded from the efficiency discussion.

strengths: The coarse-to-fine sampling idea is intuitive and practically relevant, particularly for diffusion transformers whose attention cost grows rapidly with spatial resolution.

The method delivers substantial measured efficiency gains: scale-wise variants are about twice as fast as corresponding full-resolution variants in the reported setup, with similarly reduced training-iteration time.
Experiments cover two modern text-to-image backbones, multiple automatic metrics, human comparisons, runtime measurements, and several useful ablations.

The comparison with full-resolution training helps isolate the effect of scale-wise generation, while the time-shift, scale-schedule, scale-wise-training, and PDM ablations indicate that each design choice affects performance.
Training one model across resolutions and using ordinary bicubic interpolation makes the sampling procedure relatively simple and potentially easy to integrate into existing distillation pipelines.
weaknesses: The central claim that high-noise latent diffusion can operate at lower resolution "without information loss" is not established. The evidence consists mainly of radially averaged spectra at selected timesteps, with no stated sample size, uncertainty, aliasing analysis, or quantitative criterion connecting spectral energy to the chosen scale and timestep schedules. The schedules consequently appear hand-designed rather than derived from the analysis.

The proposed PDM objective is conceptually underspecified and arguably mischaracterized. Equation 2 compares per-image averages of teacher features for paired real and generated samples; this is closer to paired feature-mean matching than MMD between overall patch distributions. The RBF estimator, kernel bandwidth, feature normalization, loss coefficients, and complete combined objective are not reported.

Several conclusions overstate the results. At matched step counts in Table 2, scale-wise generation has worse FID than the full-scale alternative in every reported comparison. In Table 4, SWD improves preference-model metrics but has substantially worse FID than multiple baselines—for example, 23.0 versus 7.2 on COCO for SWD/M versus DMD2-SDXL—so the broad claim of outperforming state-of-the-art models is not supported consistently.

The human evaluation is too weakly reported to resolve these conflicting metrics. It uses only 128 prompts, presents most results graphically without exact preference rates, and does not provide confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement, assessor counts, or a clear treatment of ties and repeated judgments. Claims such as "significant gap" are therefore unsupported.

Baseline comparability is limited. Methods use different architectures, parameter counts, teachers, and potentially implementation stacks, while the paper does not adequately document how baseline outputs and latency numbers were obtained or whether generation settings were optimized comparably. This weakens both quality and speed rankings.

The ablations do not cleanly establish the novelty or generality of PDM. Removing PDM causes unusually large changes, yet sensitivity to its weight and feature layer is absent; the standalone PDM model remains considerably worse than the combined method; and evaluation is confined to the same model family and synthetic-data pipeline used to develop the method.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier paper. Prompt sources for the 500K synthetic training samples, preprocessing, loss weights, optimizer details, training-time schedule sampling, random seeds, checkpoint selection, and several model-specific discriminator details are missing. There is also no clear code, checkpoint, or generated-dataset release commitment.

The novelty positioning is incomplete: closely related progressive-resolution diffusion and distillation work, including PAGODA and multiscale/cascaded diffusion, is cited but not compared experimentally or distinguished sharply enough from the proposed contribution.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and broader-impact discussion despite addressing text-to-image generation, including potential dataset bias, harmful content, misuse, and the implications of distilling teacher behavior.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, practically meaningful contribution: progressively increasing spatial resolution during few-step diffusion sampling reduces redundant high-resolution computation while retaining substantially more denoising capacity than an equally fast full-resolution sampler.

The method is well motivated by spectral analysis of latent diffusion processes, and the proposed upsample-then-noise design is supported by a targeted experiment showing that it aligns much better with full-resolution noisy latents than directly upsampling noisy latents.

The evaluation is broad and generally convincing: it covers two SD3.5 model sizes, COCO and MJHQ, multiple automated metrics, professional human evaluation, latency and training cost, full-resolution controls, existing distilled and next-scale baselines, and qualitative comparisons.

The efficiency gains are substantial. At the same step count, SWD approximately halves inference latency (e.g., 0.17 versus 0.38 seconds for six-step SD3.5 Medium) and also reduces per-iteration training time, while most semantic and preference metrics remain comparable or improve.

The ablations establish that scale-wise training, timestep shifting, progressive rather than abrupt scale changes, synthetic teacher data, and PDM each contribute. PDM is appealing because it reuses pretrained diffusion features and requires no additional learned model when used alone.
weaknesses: The quality-efficiency tradeoff is less uniformly favorable than the presentation suggests. SWD has substantially worse FID than several baselines and teachers—for example, 23.0 on COCO versus 14.3 for DMD2-SDXL and 16.4 for SD3.5 Medium. Improvements are concentrated in preference-model metrics and image complexity, while human advantages in relevance, aesthetics, and defects are often small or mixed.

The PDM formulation is somewhat oversold as matching patch distributions. With the linear kernel, Equation 2 only matches the spatially averaged feature vector of each paired image; it does not directly preserve the distribution or spatial organization of individual tokens. The standalone PDM result is also materially below the complete method, so claims of competitiveness should be qualified.

The human evaluation uses only 128 prompts and two images per prompt. Although three judgments and confidence intervals are provided, the paper does not report numerical preference rates, assessor agreement, significance tests, or sensitivity to seeds and prompt selection, making close comparisons around 50% difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as the relative weights of reverse-KL, GAN, and PDM losses, optimizer settings, the discriminator setup for SD3.5 Large, precise data construction, random seeds, and the procedure used to select timestep and scale schedules are missing. No code or model-release commitment is stated.

The spectral argument is primarily qualitative and examines selected models and timesteps. A quantitative link between discarded spectral energy and the chosen scale schedule, or experiments deriving schedules from the analysis rather than manual selection, would make the central motivation substantially stronger.

Baseline comparisons are not perfectly controlled for model size, architecture, training data, or optimization, and synthetic-teacher dataset generation cost is excluded from the training-efficiency discussion. Thus, the strongest evidence is the controlled comparison with the paper's own full-resolution variant rather than the broader state-of-the-art ranking.

strengths: The progressive spatial-and-temporal resolution strategy is a clear, practically meaningful contribution: it exploits the coarse-to-fine behavior of diffusion sampling while retaining a single model and diffusion process.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering four major text-to-image model families and a text-to-video model, with controlled full-resolution counterparts that isolate the benefit of scale-wise sampling.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial: approximately 2x for image models and 3x for video at the same number of steps, while quality is generally maintained or improved. Compute-matched comparisons against two-step full-resolution students also favor SwD.

Evaluation combines large-sample automatic metrics, human preference judgments, runtime measurements, high-frequency patch metrics, and qualitative examples. The video experiments further test both spatial-only and spatiotemporal scaling.

The paper includes useful ablations of the MMD objective, progressive versus constant scale schedules, latent upsampling order, and MMD-only training. The result that the inexpensive fixed-feature loss can work without auxiliary trainable models is practically valuable.
The method is clearly motivated by spectral measurements across several image and video latent spaces, and the exposition is generally coherent and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details are absent, including the number and prompt distribution of synthetic training samples, optimizer and scheduler settings, loss weights alpha and beta, sampling distributions for loss timesteps, update ratios for generator/fake model/discriminator, and random-seed variability. No usable project or code link is provided in the manuscript.

The proposed linear-kernel “MMD” reduces to a squared distance between per-image spatial-feature means. This is closer to paired feature matching over patches than conventional distribution-level MMD over samples. The distinction, assumptions about pairing teacher targets with student outputs, and possible pressure toward conditional feature means deserve more precise treatment.

The spectral analysis is primarily motivational: its plotted frequency boundaries are heuristic, and the actual scale/timestep schedules remain manually chosen hyperparameters. The claim that performance is not highly sensitive to schedule choice is not supported by a systematic sensitivity study.

Comparisons to other progressive-resolution or adaptive-compute diffusion methods are limited, despite several closely related approaches being discussed. Most headline comparisons instead concern fixed-resolution distilled models, so the incremental advantage over the nearest progressive-generation alternatives is not fully established.

The human evaluation uses only 128 prompts with two generations per prompt and three judgments per pair. Numerical preference rates, confidence intervals, assessor agreement, randomization procedures, and significance tests are not reported clearly enough to substantiate small claimed differences.

Runtime results use batch size eight, torch.compile, FP16, and replacement TinyVAEs, then report average time divided by batch size. This is useful throughput evidence but does not establish interactive batch-one latency, memory usage, or behavior with the original VAE; these qualifications should accompany the headline speedups.
Results are reported for single training runs without uncertainty. Some metric improvements are small, making it difficult to determine whether they are robust to training and sampling variance.

The paper does not discuss broader risks specific to accelerating high-quality image/video generation, such as misuse, bias, provenance, or deployment safeguards, beyond describing the treatment of human assessors.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically meaningful contribution: progressive spatial and temporal resolution within a single few-step diffusion model, reducing computation without requiring a cascade of separately trained models.
The proposed sampling mechanism—upsampling the clean prediction before re-noising—is simple, well motivated, and empirically supported by comparisons against alternative transition strategies.
The empirical scope is unusually broad: the method is evaluated on four major text-to-image model families and a text-to-video model, with both automatic metrics and professional human evaluation.

The reported efficiency gains are substantial. Scale-wise sampling is approximately 2× faster for image generation and 3× faster for video generation than equal-step full-resolution counterparts, while generally preserving quality; comparisons at matched latency favor the proposed approach more clearly.

The paper includes meaningful component studies, including scale-wise versus full-resolution sampling, progressive versus nearly constant scale schedules, spatial-plus-temporal versus spatial-only video scaling, high-frequency-detail metrics, and several variants of the proposed feature-matching objective.

The MMD-inspired objective is computationally attractive and practically useful: it can operate without adversarial or learned fake-score models, reduces training iteration time substantially, and remains competitive when used alone.
The paper is clearly organized, and the appendices provide schedules, training settings, runtime methodology, expanded quantitative results, qualitative comparisons, and human-evaluation procedures.
weaknesses: The spectral analysis provides intuition rather than a principled derivation of the scale schedules. The authors explicitly leave both timestep and scale schedules as hyperparameters, and the claim that frequency masking identifies safe resolutions is not validated causally or per sample.

The purported linear-kernel MMD objective reduces to per-image squared distance between mean spatial features of paired real and generated samples. This is closer to perceptual feature matching than distribution matching across samples, making the MMD framing and associated novelty somewhat overstated.

Comparisons against other progressive-computation approaches are incomplete. Several closely related dynamic-resolution or token-reduction methods are discussed or cited, but the principal experiments mainly compare against fixed-resolution distilled models rather than controlled implementations of these efficiency alternatives.

Some central quality differences are small and lack uncertainty estimates. The paper reports no variance across training runs, confidence intervals for automatic metrics, or statistical significance for most comparisons; this matters particularly when score differences are only a few tenths.

The video evidence is narrower than the image evidence: it uses one relatively small base model, one main distilled baseline, and no human evaluation of temporal quality. Thus, broad claims about text-to-video applicability are less convincingly supported.

The human study uses only 128 prompts, and the paper does not clearly report inter-annotator agreement or statistical tests. Its four separately judged criteria are useful, but they do not fully establish overall preference or video quality.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details: dataset sizes and release status, loss weights, optimizer settings, random seeds, and training-run variability are not specified, and the project-page link in the manuscript is blank.

Latency is measured with batch size 8, torch.compile, and replacement TinyVAEs. Although these choices are applied broadly, additional batch-1 measurements and a clearer accounting of whether every public baseline received identical compilation and decoder treatment would make the deployment claims more robust.
The paper gives little discussion of safety implications or misuse risks associated with making high-capacity image and video generators substantially faster.

strengths: The central systems idea is clear and practically important: progressive spatial/temporal scaling attacks a compute axis complementary to reducing denoising steps, and the proposed upsample-denoise-renoise construction fits naturally into stochastic few-step sampling.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: SwD is tested on four major text-to-image model families and a text-to-video model, with teacher, distilled, autoregressive, fixed-resolution, and compute-matched comparisons. The reported speedups are substantial and supported by a reasonably controlled latency protocol.

Evidence for the principal claim is convincing. Same-step scale-wise versus full-resolution comparisons isolate the value of progressive scaling, while compute-matched comparisons show clear quality advantages over simply using fewer full-resolution steps. Automatic metrics, professional human judgments, qualitative results, patch metrics, and ablations generally agree.

The feature-space MMD objective is simple, inexpensive, and practically useful. Its strong standalone performance, much lower training-iteration cost, design ablations, and analysis of cases where DMD fails make it a meaningful additional contribution.

The paper is well written and visually clear. It reports schedules, optimization settings, hardware, runtime methodology, and human-assessment procedures, and it candidly discusses limitations of DMD when teachers perform poorly at low resolution.
weaknesses: The spectral analysis is mainly motivational rather than predictive: there is no quantitative rule mapping spectra to scale schedules, schedules remain manually chosen hyperparameters, and robustness is examined through only a limited schedule comparison. Broader sensitivity analysis or automatic schedule selection would strengthen the claimed connection.

With the selected linear kernel, the proposed “MMD” averages spatial tokens separately within each image and becomes an MSE between feature means. This resembles per-example feature matching more than conventional distribution matching across independent samples, making the novelty and distributional interpretation somewhat overstated.

The human evaluation does not clearly report exact preference rates, statistical significance or confidence intervals, assessor counts, or agreement statistics. The video study has no human evaluation and covers only one relatively small base video model, so its strongest quality claims depend on learned metrics.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the manuscript does not commit to releasing code or models, the project-page field is blank, and the exact synthetic training-set size and prompt composition are not specified. Teacher-data generation cost is also omitted from the efficiency analysis.

Runtime is measured only on one A100 using batch size eight, FP16, compilation, and substituted TinyVAEs. Batch-one latency, memory, FLOPs, other hardware, and end-to-end costs including teacher-data generation would make the efficiency conclusions more portable.
